A human-on-a-chip is the proposed integration of multiple organ models into a connected system that reproduces important body-wide signaling and drug distribution. Fluid connections could reveal effects that appear only after one tissue transforms a compound used by another.

Major barriers include missing organ models, scaling relationships, and the lack of one culture medium that supports all tissues simultaneously.

10506.title: Human-Computer Interaction
10506.heading: Human-Computer Interaction
10506.content:
Human-computer interaction studies the relationship and communication between people and interactive technology. People communicate actions, goals, and queries to a system, while the system communicates its state and responses through a [[User Interface]].

The field places human needs first and draws on knowledge of [[Perception]], [[Cognition]], and physical action. It includes both understanding existing interactions and designing new ones, from devices and gestures to computer-mediated collaboration. Effectiveness depends on the purpose: task performance may dominate a work system, while engagement or emotional impact may matter more in a game or artwork.

HCI design therefore involves tradeoffs rather than a single universally optimal solution.

10509.sourceSearchName: human centered ai human centered ai
10509.title: Human-Centered AI
10509.heading: Human-Centered AI
10509.content:
Human-centered AI directs the design and governance of artificial intelligence toward human dignity, agency, rights, and well-being. It rejects systems that make people serve technical optimization and requires that important automated processes remain answerable to those they affect.

The approach is valuable when it protects people from manipulation or unaccountable power, but its scope is contested. A strictly human-centric policy can neglect animals, ecosystems, and the material conditions on which human life depends. [[Anthropocentrism in AI Ethics]] identifies this limit, while [[Sustainable AI]] expands the account of responsible design beyond immediate human users.

10512.heading: Human-Computer Teaming
10512.content:
Human-computer teaming assigns complementary parts of a task to people and machines. Computers contribute speed, search, and consistent calculation, while people contribute context, judgment, meaning, and the ability to respond to unforeseen situations.

A team is not automatically better than either member alone. Performance depends on interface design, division of authority, shared awareness, and whether human intervention occurs at a point where it can still affect the outcome.

10515.heading: Human-AI Collaboration
10515.content:
Human-AI collaboration divides activity between machine pattern recognition and human judgment, experience, or responsibility. It can use automation to extend human capability without assuming that either partner should perform the whole task.

The arrangement is ethical only when the human role is substantive. A person who must approve opaque outputs at machine speed may provide the appearance of oversight without real control. Good collaboration preserves the knowledge, time, authority, and feedback needed to question the system. It also recognizes that practical wisdom and contextual understanding cannot simply be delegated to statistical prediction.

10518.heading: Human Security Layer
10518.content:
The human security layer addresses the decisions, habits, and social interactions through which people affect a system's security. Training, clear procedures, careful identity verification, and usable controls reduce the chance that a person becomes the easiest route around technical defenses.

Because attackers can exploit trust through [[Social Engineering]], this layer belongs inside [[Defense in Depth]] rather than outside the technical system. Security design must account for how people actually work.

10521.title: Human Factors
10521.heading: Human Factors
10521.content:
Human factors are the capabilities, characteristics, and limitations of the person using a system. They include the body acting, the senses perceiving, and the brain thinking.

Human-factors-driven design studies what people can comfortably and reliably do, then uses that knowledge to pursue safe, efficient, and effective interaction. In a [[3D User Interface]], relevant areas include [[Perception]], [[Cognition]], [[Attention]], and [[Physical Ergonomics]]. These factors are interconnected, so evaluation may need to isolate particular issues without forgetting their relationships.

Human factors form a foundation for [[User-Centered Design]] and [[Usability Engineering]].

10524.title: Human Exceptionalism in AI
10524.heading: Human Exceptionalism in AI
10524.content:
Human exceptionalism in AI is the belief that a morally decisive boundary separates humans from machines. The boundary may be grounded in consciousness, reason, emotion, embodiment, free will, or participation in human social life.

AI makes the belief difficult to apply because machines can imitate individual capacities without clearly possessing the whole form of life associated with them. Rejecting exceptionalism does not require treating every machine as a person. It instead requires explaining why a particular capacity or relationship matters and recognizing that nonhuman beings may have value without duplicating humanity.

These teams anticipated modern distributed systems. Their practices exposed the importance of decomposition, communication patterns, synchronization, and verification long before those ideas were implemented in electronic hardware.

10551.content:
HTTP Strict Transport Security is a response policy that tells a browser to use HTTPS for a host for a defined period. After receiving the policy over a valid secure connection, the browser upgrades later HTTP attempts instead of first sending an insecure request.

HSTS reduces downgrade and first-request exposure after the policy is known. It does not replace a valid TLS certificate or correct server-side HTTPS configuration.

10602.content:
Hot cloud storage is optimized for data that is accessed frequently. Its storage cost is higher than a colder tier, while reading and writing the data is comparatively less expensive.

The photo project uses hot storage during development and testing because files are repeatedly exercised. Tier selection should follow the expected access pattern rather than the file type alone.

10605.title: Householder Transformation
10605.heading: Householder Transformation
10605.content:
A Householder transformation is an orthogonal reflection of the form $H=I-2uu^T/(u^Tu)$. It maps a vector onto a chosen coordinate direction and can zero many entries at once.

Successive reflections reduce a symmetric matrix to tridiagonal form or a general matrix toward Hessenberg form, preparing it for a [[QR Algorithm]].

10608.title: Hovmoller Diagram
10608.heading: Hovmoller Diagram
10608.content: A Hovmoller diagram places time on one axis, a spatial coordinate or zone on the other, and an aggregated field value in color. It reduces one spatial dimension of a [[Space-Time Raster]], making propagation, seasonality, and persistent bands visible in a single panel. The aggregation direction and function must be stated because distinct geographic patterns can produce the same reduced matrix.

10611.content:
Host-based malware relies on another file, application, or execution context. A [[Computer Virus]] attaches itself to a host, while a [[Trojan Horse Malware]] disguises malicious behavior inside an apparently useful program and a [[Logic Bomb Malware]] waits for a triggering condition.

Because this family depends on trusted or legitimate-looking contexts, controlling software execution, inspecting content, limiting privileges, and helping users recognize deceptive delivery are important defenses.

The result should not be treated as a permanent one-to-one identity. A name can change addresses, provide several addresses, or fail to resolve, so connection code must handle those outcomes explicitly.

10626.content: Horizontal scaling changes the number of application instances rather than the size of one instance. A load balancer distributes requests among several servers, increasing aggregate capacity and allowing one node to fail without necessarily ending the service. The application must handle session state and shared data deliberately; requests tied to one server through sticky sessions limit how evenly load can be spread.

10629.content:
Hospital big data includes clinical, administrative, treatment, timing, demographic, and operational records accumulated through everyday care. It is large, high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and often noisy because it was collected for many immediate purposes rather than one later model.

Operational analytics can extract queue and duration patterns, but interpretation must respect clinical meaning, provenance, privacy, and missing observations.

10632.title: Horizontal Scalability
10632.heading: Horizontal Scalability
10632.content:
Horizontal scalability changes capacity by changing the number of comparable resource instances. Scaling out adds servers or service instances to meet greater demand; scaling in releases them when the demand recedes.

Unlike [[Vertical Scalability]], the individual resource does not have to become more powerful. [[Rapid Elasticity]] applies horizontal scaling dynamically in both directions, normally using pooled and virtualized resources.

10638.title: Horizontal Asymptote
10638.heading: Horizontal Asymptote
10638.content: The line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f$ when $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ tends to positive or negative infinity. It describes end behavior, not a barrier: a graph may cross the line at finite inputs. A function can have different horizontal asymptotes in its two infinite directions.

10641.title: Horizon Graph
10641.heading: Horizon Graph
10641.content: A horizon graph divides positive and negative deviations into magnitude bands, mirrors the negative bands, and overlays the bands within a compact strip. Hue distinguishes sign while color intensity distinguishes magnitude. This compression lets many time series appear as vertically aligned [[Time-Series Small Multiples]] without losing broad changes. Exact values are difficult to recover, so a horizon graph is best for pattern comparison rather than precise reading.

Commonality makes these processes strong candidates for standardization and [[Business Process as a Service]]. A provider can spread the cost of a repeatable workflow across consumers while exposing the interfaces each organization needs.

A common scale supports comparison among panels because the same intensity means the same deviation everywhere. Panel-specific scales expose each series' internal variation but prevent direct magnitude comparison. The choice must match the question and be stated clearly, because the compact encoding of a [[Horizon Graph]] makes an unnoticed scale change especially misleading.

Windows and other geometric discontinuities must avoid sharp stress concentrations.

Homology vanishes at a position exactly when the complex is exact there. A [[Short Exact Sequence of Complexes]] produces a [[Long Exact Sequence in Homology]] that relates the homology of all three complexes.

Homothetic divisive clustering splits a data set using one binary variable at a time so that a chosen within- or between-group criterion improves. The process continues with other variables until a stopping rule is met.

10662.title: Homoscedasticity
10662.heading: Homoscedasticity
10662.content:
Homoscedasticity means that the variance of regression errors is constant across fitted values and predictor levels. It supports the conventional standard errors and significance tests of ordinary linear regression.

A residual plot with changing vertical spread suggests heteroscedasticity. Large samples do not make the pattern disappear, although the substantive consequence depends on its severity and the inferential method used.

10665.title: Homography
10665.heading: Homography
10665.content:
A homography is a projective transformation that maps points on one plane to their corresponding positions in another image or plane. A square AR marker has known planar coordinates, so its four detected image corners provide enough constraints to estimate this mapping.

With a calibrated camera, the homography can be decomposed into a rotation and translation consistent with the marker plane. Noise makes the estimate approximate, which is why pose refinement may follow.

Methods can reweight source instances, learn a shared representation, or adapt model parameters toward the target. Similarity must still be assessed because matching variable names do not guarantee matching predictive relationships.

Group standard deviations, box plots, residual plots, and formal tests can inform the judgment. Formal variance tests can detect trivial departures in very large samples, so statistical significance should be considered alongside the size and practical consequence of the difference.

Quotienting a [[Graded Ring]] by a homogeneous ideal preserves a grading. Extension and contraction along graded homomorphisms also preserve homogeneity under the source's conditions.

10683.heading: Homogeneous Element
10683.content:
A homogeneous element of a [[Graded Ring]] or graded module belongs to one degree component. Multiplying homogeneous elements adds their degrees.

Every element is a finite sum of homogeneous components. Homogeneous generators let ideals, modules, and resolutions be studied degree by degree rather than only as undifferentiated algebraic objects.

10686.title: Homeostasis
10686.heading: Homeostasis
10686.content:
Homeostasis is a system's ability to maintain internal conditions within a narrow range despite changes in its environment. It is an adaptive form of dynamic balance rather than a perfectly static state.

Homeostatic [[Balancing Loop|balancing loops]] make a system resilient within limits. If disturbances exceed the system's ability to rebalance, it can become brittle and cross a point from which it cannot recover.

10707.heading: Holdout Mattes in Layered Composites
10707.content: When a foreground element covers part of a background, the foreground's matte identifies where it contributes and a complementary holdout removes that same region from the background. A holdout dataset is a subset excluded from a particular fitting stage so it can estimate performance on unseen cases. Depending on the workflow, a holdout may serve as validation or final testing.

Its interpretation depends on randomization, representativeness, and a strict record of which decisions were allowed to use it.

10716.title: HiveQL
10716.heading: HiveQL
10716.content:
HiveQL is the SQL-like query language of [[Apache Hive]]. Its statements describe tables, filters, joins, grouping, aggregation, and nested transformations over distributed data.

Hive parses a query, checks it against the metastore, optimizes a logical plan, and generates a physical plan for Hadoop execution. The familiar relational syntax lowers the barrier for analysts accustomed to SQL.

10719.sourceSearchName: historical bias in data historical bias in data
10719.title: Historical Bias in Data
10719.heading: Historical Bias in Data
10719.content:
Historical bias in data occurs when records encode earlier discrimination, exclusion, or unequal access. A model can learn this pattern accurately and then present its continuation as an objective prediction.

The problem remains even if collection and computation are technically correct. Data describing the world as it was do not decide whether the world should remain that way. In hiring, policing, or lending, past outcomes may reflect unequal opportunity rather than differences relevant to future decisions. Addressing the bias requires normative choices about correction, not merely a larger sample of the same history.

10720.sourceSearchName: historical bias in data historical bias in data
10720.title: Historical Bias in Data
10720.heading: References

10722.title: Histogram
10722.heading: Histogram
10722.content:
A histogram displays the distribution of a continuous variable by dividing its range into intervals and drawing a bar for the frequency or proportion in each interval. It reveals concentration, skewness, gaps, and possible outliers.

The choice of breaks can change the apparent shape, so it should be explored rather than treated as neutral. Axis limits and labels should reflect the valid measurement range, especially after special missing codes have been removed.

10725.title: Histogram of Oriented Gradients Descriptor
10725.heading: Histogram of Oriented Gradients Descriptor
10725.content:
A histogram of oriented gradients descriptor summarizes the directions and strengths of local intensity changes around an image feature. Pooling gradient orientations into spatial cells produces a compact representation of neighborhood shape that is less sensitive to small pixel changes than direct comparison.

In clone detection, similar descriptors identify potential source-and-copy feature pairs even after modest processing. A descriptor match is only a candidate because unrelated repeated structures can look alike; its geometric relationship and underlying pixels must also agree.

More generally, HOG partitions an image into spatial cells, accumulates local gradient orientations, and normalizes neighboring cells in blocks. This preserves coarse shape and edge layout while reducing sensitivity to absolute illumination.

10728.title: Hilbert-Samuel Polynomial
10728.heading: Hilbert-Samuel Polynomial
10728.content:
For an ideal of definition I in a Noetherian local ring and a finite module M, the length ℓ(M/IⁿM) agrees with a polynomial in n for all sufficiently large n. This is the Hilbert-Samuel polynomial.

Its degree is the [[Dimension of a Module]]. Its leading coefficient, after normalization by a factorial, defines the [[Hilbert-Samuel Multiplicity]].

10731.title: Hill Shading
10731.heading: Hill Shading
10731.content: Hill shading simulates illumination over a digital elevation model by deriving slope and aspect and calculating how each surface faces an assumed light source. The resulting grayscale relief can sit beneath a translucent thematic raster or support a [[Physical Map]]. It communicates terrain form rather than measured brightness. Light direction and vertical exaggeration affect the apparent shape, so the shading should remain context instead of competing with the mapped variable.

10734.title: Hill Climbing
10734.heading: Hill Climbing
10734.content:
Hill climbing is a problem-solving approach that repeatedly moves from the current solution to a better neighboring solution. The metaphor treats the desired optimum as a peak and each allowed change as a step on the terrain.

Because it uses only local improvement, hill climbing can stop at a [[Local Optimum]] or plateau that is lower than the [[Global Optimum]]. Escaping may require returning to an earlier state or using a strategy that accepts a move without immediate improvement.

10737.title: Hilbert-Samuel Multiplicity
10737.heading: Hilbert-Samuel Multiplicity
10737.content:
The Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity e(I,M) is the factorial-normalized leading coefficient of the [[Hilbert-Samuel Polynomial]] for ℓ(M/IⁿM). It measures the leading growth of lengths along powers of an ideal of definition.

For a local ring or module, this multiplicity refines dimension with quantitative information about the local algebra. It also appears in formulas for parametrized surfaces with base points.

10740.title: Hilbert Series
10740.heading: Hilbert Series
10740.content:
The Hilbert series of a bounded-below graded module is the formal series P_M(t) = ΣH_M(n)tⁿ. Its coefficients are the values of the [[Hilbert Function]].

For finitely generated graded modules over Noetherian graded rings, the source shows that this series is rational. Free resolutions express it as an alternating combination of shifted free-module series.

10743.title: Hilbert Syzygy Theorem
10743.heading: Hilbert Syzygy Theorem
10743.content:
The graded Hilbert syzygy theorem states that every finitely generated graded module over K[x₁,…,xₙ] has a finite graded free resolution of length at most n.

Any two minimal graded resolutions are isomorphic. Thus polynomial rings impose a uniform bound on how many successive layers of [[Syzygy Module]]s are needed to describe a finitely generated module.

10746.title: Hilbert Function
10746.heading: Hilbert Function
10746.content:
For a graded module M whose degree pieces have finite length over R₀, the Hilbert function is H_M(n) = ℓ(Mₙ). It counts the algebraic size available in each degree.

For a finitely generated module over a standard graded polynomial ring, the function eventually agrees with a [[Hilbert Polynomial]]. Encoding all values as coefficients of a generating function gives the [[Hilbert Series]].

10749.title: Hilbert Polynomial
10749.heading: Hilbert Polynomial
10749.content:
The Hilbert polynomial is the polynomial that agrees with the [[Hilbert Function]] of a finitely generated graded module for all sufficiently large degrees.

Over a standard graded polynomial ring, its degree is one less than the [[Dimension of a Module]] when the module is not Artinian. Its leading coefficient records the module's multiplicity after factorial normalization.

10752.title: Hilbert Basis Theorem
10752.heading: Hilbert Basis Theorem
10752.content:
The Hilbert basis theorem states that if R is a [[Noetherian Ring]], then R[x] is also Noetherian. Iterating the result shows that a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field is Noetherian.

Consequently every polynomial ideal has a finite generating set, and every finitely generated algebra over a field is Noetherian. This finiteness is essential for Gröbner-basis computation.
